verses.zh: 书亚人比勒达回答说：
verses.en: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered:

verses.zh: 你寻索言语要到几时呢？你可以揣摩思想，然后我们就说话。
verses.en: “How long until you[NOTE:1] make an end of words?[NOTE:2] You must consider,[NOTE:3] and then[NOTE:4] we can talk.
notes: Bildad attacks Job with less subtlety than Eliphaz. He describes the miserable existence of the wicked, indicating that it is the proof of sin. His speech falls into two main parts: why is Job so contemptuous toward his friends (Job 18:2-4), and the fate of the wicked (18:5-21). On this chapter see N. M. Sarna, “The Mythological Background of Job 18,” JBL 82 (1963): 315-18; and W. A. Irwin, “Job’s Redeemer,” JBL 81 (1962): 217-29.
The verb is plural, and so most commentators make it singular. But it seems from the context that Bildad is addressing all of them, and not just Job.

The construction is קִנְצֵי לְמִלִּין (qintse lemillin), which is often taken to be “end of words,” as if the word was from קֵץ (qets, “end”). But a plural of “end” is not found in the OT. Some will link the word to Arabic qanasa, “to hunt; to give chase,” to get an interpretation of “snares for words.” But E. Dhorme (Job, 257) objects that this does not fit the speech of Bildad (as well as it might Job’s). He finds a cognate qinsu, “fetters, shackles,” and reads “how long will you put shackles on words.” But G. R. Driver had pointed out that this cognate does not exist (“Problems in the Hebrew text of Job,” VTSup 3 [1955]: 72-93). So it would be preferable to take the reading “ends” and explain the ן (nun) as from a Aramaizing by-form. This is supported by 11QtgJob that uses סוֹף (sof, “end”). On the construction, GKC 421 §130.a explains this as a use of the construct in rapid narrative to connect the words; in such cases a preposition is on the following noun.

The imperfect verb, again plural, would be here taken in the nuance of instruction, or a modal nuance of obligation. So Bildad is telling his listeners to be intelligent. This would be rather cutting in the discourse.

verses.zh: 我们为何算为畜生，在你眼中看作污秽呢？
verses.en: Why should we be regarded as beasts,and considered stupid[NOTE:1] in your sight?
notes: Heb “afterward.”

verses.zh: 你这恼怒将自己撕裂的，难道大地为你见弃、磐石挪开原处吗？
verses.en: You who tear yourself[NOTE:1] to pieces in your anger,will the earth be abandoned[NOTE:2] for your sake?Or will a rock be moved from its place?[NOTE:3]
notes: The verb נִטְמִינוּ (nitminu) has been explained from different roots. Some take it from תָּמֵא (tameʾ, “to be unclean”), and translate it “Why should we be unclean in your eyes?” Most would connect it to טָמַם (tamam, “to stop up”), meaning “to be stupid” in the Niphal. Another suggestion is to follow the LXX and read from דָּמַם (damam, “to be reduced to silence”). Others take it from דָּמָּה (damah) with a meaning “to be like.” But what is missing is the term of comparison—like what? Various suggestions have been made, but all are simply conjectures.

The construction uses the participle and then third person suffixes: “O tearer of himself in his anger.” But it is clearly referring to Job, and so the direct second person pronouns should be used to make that clear. The LXX is an approximation or paraphrase here: “Anger has possessed you, for what if you should die—would under heaven be desolate, or shall the mountains be overthrown from their foundations?”

There is a good deal of study on this word in this passage, and in Job in general. M. Dahood suggested a root עָזַב (ʿazav) meaning “to arrange; to rearrange” (“The Root ʿzb II in Job,” JBL 78 [1959]: 303-9). But this is refuted by H. G. M. Williamson, “A Reconsideration of ʿzb II in Biblical Hebrew,” ZAW 97 (1985): 74-85.

verses.zh: 恶人的亮光必要熄灭；他的火焰必不照耀。
verses.en: “Yes,[NOTE:1] the lamp[NOTE:2] of the wicked is extinguished;his flame of fire[NOTE:3] does not shine.
notes: Bildad is asking if Job thinks the whole moral order of the world should be interrupted for his sake, that he may escape the punishment for wickedness.
Hebrew גַּם (gam, “also; moreover”), in view of what has just been said.
The lamp or the light can have a number of uses in the Bible. Here it is probably an implied metaphor for prosperity and happiness, for the good life itself.

verses.zh: 他帐棚中的亮光要变为黑暗；他以上的灯也必熄灭。
verses.en: The light in his tent grows dark;his lamp above him is extinguished.[NOTE:1]
notes: The expression is literally “the flame of his fire,” but the pronominal suffix qualifies the entire bound construction. The two words together intensify the idea of the flame.

verses.zh: 他坚强的脚步必见狭窄；自己的计谋必将他绊倒。
verses.en: His vigorous steps[NOTE:1] are restricted,[NOTE:2] and his own counsel throws him down.[NOTE:3]
notes: The LXX interprets a little more precisely: “his lamp shall be put out with him.”sn This thesis of Bildad will be questioned by Job in 21:17—how often is the lamp of the wicked snuffed out?
Heb “the steps of his vigor,” the genitive being the attribute.

The verb צָרַר (tsarar) means “to be cramped; to be straitened; to be hemmed in.” The trouble has hemmed him in, so that he cannot walk with the full, vigorous steps he had before. The LXX has “Let the meanest of men spoil his goods.”

verses.zh: 因为他被自己的脚陷入网中，走在缠人的网罗上。
verses.en: For he has been thrown into a net by his feet,[NOTE:1] and he wanders into a mesh.[NOTE:2]
notes: The LXX has “causes him to stumble,” which many commentators accept, but this involves the transposition of the three letters. The verb is שָׁלַךְ (shalakh, “throw”) not כָּשַׁל (kashal, “stumble”).
See Ps 25:15.

verses.zh: 圈套必抓住他的脚跟；机关必擒获他。
verses.en: A trap[NOTE:1] seizes him by the heel;a snare[NOTE:2] grips him.
notes: The word שְׂבָכָה (sevakhah) is used in scripture for the lattice window (2 Kgs 1:2). The Arabic cognate means “to be intertwined.” So the term could describe a net, matting, grating, or lattice. Here it would be the netting stretched over a pit.
This word פָּח (pakh) specifically refers to the snare of the fowler—thus a bird trap. But its plural seems to refer to nets in general (see Job 22:10).

verses.zh: 活扣为他藏在土内；羁绊为他藏在路上。
verses.en: A rope is hidden for him[NOTE:1] on the ground,and a trap for him[NOTE:2] lies on the path.
notes: This word does not occur elsewhere. But another word from the same root means “plait of hair,” and so this term has something to do with a net like a trellis or lattice.
Heb “his rope.” The suffix must be a genitive expressing that the trap was for him, to trap him, and so an objective genitive.

verses.zh: 四面的惊吓要使他害怕，并且追赶他的脚跟。
verses.en: Terrors[NOTE:1] frighten him on all sidesand dog[NOTE:2] his every step.
notes: Heb “his trap.” The pronominal suffix is objective genitive here as well.
Bildad is referring here to all the things that afflict a person and cause terror. It would then be a metonymy of effect, the cause being the afflictions.

verses.zh: 他的力量必因饥饿衰败；祸患要在他旁边等候。
verses.en: Calamity is[NOTE:1] hungry for him,[NOTE:2] and misfortune is ready at his side.[NOTE:3]
notes: The verb פּוּץ (puts) in the Hiphil has the meaning “to pursue” and “to scatter.” It is followed by the expression “at his feet.” So the idea is easily derived: they chase him at his feet. But some commentators have other proposals. The most far-fetched is that of Ehrlich and Driver (ZAW 24 [1953]: 259-60) which has “and compel him to urinate on his feet,” one of many similar readings the NEB accepted from Driver.
The jussive is occasionally used without its normal sense and only as an imperfect (see GKC 323 §109.k).
There are a number of suggestions for אֹנוֹ (ʾono). Some take it as “vigor”: thus “his strength is hungry.” Others take it as “iniquity”: thus “his iniquity/trouble is hungry.”

verses.zh: 他本身的肢体要被吞吃；死亡的长子要吞吃他的肢体。
verses.en: It eats away parts of his skin;[NOTE:1] the most terrible death[NOTE:2] devours his limbs.
notes: The expression means that misfortune is right there to destroy him whenever there is the opportunity.

The expression “the limbs of his skin” makes no sense, unless a poetic meaning of “parts” (or perhaps “layers”) is taken. The parallelism has “his skin” in the first colon, and “his limbs” in the second. One plausible suggestion is to take בַּדֵּי (badde, “limbs of”) in the first part to be בִּדְוָי (bidvay, “by a disease”; Dhorme, Wright, RSV). The verb has to be made passive, however. The versions have different things: The LXX has “let the branches of his feet be eaten”; the Syriac has “his cities will be swallowed up by force”; the Vulgate reads “let it devour the beauty of his skin”; and Targum Job has “it will devour the linen garments that cover his skin.”

verses.zh: 他要从所倚靠的帐棚被拔出来，带到惊吓的王那里。
verses.en: He is dragged from the security of his tent,[NOTE:1] and marched off[NOTE:2] to the king of terrors.[NOTE:3]
notes: The “firstborn of death” is the strongest child of death (Gen 49:3), or the deadliest death (like the “firstborn of the poor, the poorest”). The phrase means the most terrible death (A. B. Davidson, Job, 134).
Heb “from his tent, his security.” The apposition serves to modify the tent as his security.

The verb is the Hiphil of צָעַד (tsaʿad, “to lead away”). The problem is that the form is either a third feminine (Rashi thought it was referring to Job’s wife) or the second person. There is a good deal of debate over the possibility of the prefix t- being a variant for the third masculine form. The evidence in Ugaritic and Akkadian is mixed, stronger for the plural than the singular. Gesenius has some samples where the third feminine form might also be used for the passive if there is no expressed subject (see GKC 459 §144.b), but the evidence is not strong. The simplest choices are to change the prefix to a י (yod), or argue that the ת (tav) can be masculine, or follow Gesenius.

verses.zh: 不属他的必住在他的帐棚里；硫磺必撒在他所住之处。
verses.en: Fire resides in his tent;[NOTE:1] over his residence burning sulfur is scattered.
notes: This is a reference to death, the king of all terrors. Other identifications are made in the commentaries: Mot, the Ugaritic god of death; Nergal of the Babylonians; Molech of the Canaanites, the one to whom people sent emissaries.

verses.zh: 下边，他的根本要枯干；上边，他的枝子要剪除。
verses.en: Below his roots dry up,and his branches wither above.

verses.zh: 他的记念在地上必然灭亡；他的名字在街上也不存留。
verses.en: His memory perishes from the earthhe has no name in the land.[NOTE:1]
notes: This line is difficult as well. The verb, again a third feminine form, says “it dwells in his tent.” But the next part (מִבְּלִי לוֹ, mibbeli lo) means something like “things of what are not his.” The best that can be made of the MT is “There shall live in his tent they that are not his” (referring to persons and animals; see J. E. Hartley, Job [NICOT], 279). G. R. Driver and G. B. Gray (Job [ICC], 2:161) refer “that which is naught of his” to weeds and wild animals. M. Dahood suggested a reading מַבֶּל (mabbel) and a connection to Akkadian nablu, “fire” (cf. Ugaritic nbl). The interchange of m and n is not a problem, and the parallelism with the next line makes good sense (“Some Northwest Semitic words in Job,” Bib 38 [1957]: 312ff.). Others suggest an emendation to get “night-hag” or vampire. This suggestion, as well as Driver’s “mixed herbs,” are linked to the idea of exorcism. But if a change is to be made, Dahood’s is the most compelling.

verses.zh: 他必从光明中被撵到黑暗里，必被赶出世界。
verses.en: He is driven[NOTE:1] from light into darknessand is banished from the world.
notes: Heb “outside.” Cf. ESV, “in the street,” referring to absence from his community’s memory.

verses.zh: 在本民中必无子无孙；在寄居之地也无一人存留。
verses.en: He has neither children nor descendants[NOTE:1] among his people,no survivor in those places he once stayed.[NOTE:2]
notes: The verbs in this verse are plural; without the expressed subject they should be taken in the passive sense.

The two words נִין (nin, “offspring”) and נֶכֶד (nekhed, “posterity”) are always together and form an alliteration. This is hard to capture in English, but some have tried: Moffatt had “son and scion,” and Tur-Sinai had “breed or brood.” But the words are best simply translated as “lineage and posterity” or as in the NIV “offspring or descendants.”

verses.zh: 以后来的要惊奇他的日子，好像以前去的受了惊骇。
verses.en: People of the west[NOTE:1] are appalled at his fate;[NOTE:2] people of the east are seized with horror,[NOTE:3] saying,[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “in his sojournings.” The verb גּוּר (gur) means “to reside; to sojourn” temporarily, without land rights. Even this word has been selected to stress the temporary nature of his stay on earth.

The word אַחֲרֹנִים (ʾakharonim) means “those [men] coming after.” And the next word, קַדְמֹנִים (qadmonim), means “those [men] coming before.” Some commentators have tried to see here references to people who lived before and people who lived after, but that does not explain their being appalled at the fate of the wicked. So the normal way this is taken is in connection to the geography, notably the seas—“the hinder sea” refers to the Mediterranean, the West, and “the front sea” refers to the Dead Sea (Zech 14:8), namely, the East. The versions understood this as temporal: “the last groaned for him, and wonder seized the first” (LXX).
Heb “his day.”

The expression has “they seize horror.” The RSV renders this “horror seizes them.” The same idiom is found in Job 21:6: “laid hold on shuddering.” The idiom would solve the grammatical problem and not change the meaning greatly, but it would change the parallelism.

verses.zh: 不义之人的住处总是这样；此乃不认识　神之人的地步。
verses.en: ‘Surely such is the residence[NOTE:1] of an evil man;and this is the place of one who has not known God.’”[NOTE:2]
notes: The word “saying” is supplied in the translation to mark and introduce the following as a quotation of these people who are seized with horror. The alternative is to take v. 21 as Bildad’s own summary statement (cf. G. R. Driver and G. B. Gray, Job [ICC], 2:162; J. E. Hartley, Job [NICOT], 280).
The term is in the plural, “the tabernacles”; it should be taken as a plural of local extension (see GKC 397 §124.b).

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible
Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This is Bildad's second response to Job.

- He is perplexed that the suffering Job is claiming innocence and wisdom, while
experiencing such sickness and suffering. Bildad cannot accept

- Job's innocence

- an obvious violation of "the two ways" traditional theology (cf. Deut. 30:15,19; Psalm 1)

- Bildad describes, in vivid poetic imagery and parallelism, the fate of the wicked
(i.e., in this life). He thinks the poetry refers to Job but Job asserts it refers to him!

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 18:1-4
1Then
Bildad the Shuhite responded,
2"How
long will you hunt for words?
Show
understanding and then we can talk.
3Why are we
regarded as beasts,
As
stupid in your eyes?
4O
you who tear yourself in your anger—
For your sake is
the earth to be abandoned,
Or
the rock to be moved from its place?"

18:2 This verse is ambiguous in Hebrew (i.e., notice the PLURAL
when the SINGULAR would be expected, see LXX and DSS), but the
general sense is found in the TEV.

"Job, can't people like you ever be quiet?

If you stopped to listen, we could talk to you."

The MT, "set snares (BDB 890) for words," implies Job is
trying to express himself cleverly and ignore his situation. This word
is found only here in the OT. Jewish commentators took it as "end"
(AB, p. 124; NET Bible, p. 802, #27), which follows DSS (11Qtg Job) and
the LXX.

18:3 Bildad felt the sting of Job's words (i.e., Job 16:2; 17:10). Words can be like knives!
Either Job is wrong or his three friends are wrong! Who is truly "wise"? Who truly
knows God and His ways with humans?

The UBS Text Project, p. 46, has a suggested translation and interpretation,
"Bildad is addressing his friends and saying: 'Are we stopped up/impure in your eyes?'" (i.e., Job's eyes).

▣ "stupid" This VERB (BDB 380, KB 376, Niphal
PERFECT) is found only here. KB suggests it should be translated
"unclean." The LXX translates it as "silent" (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 376).
This is followed by the NJB, which has "animals" in Job 18:3a and "brutes"
in 18:3b.

18:4 Job's case is so disturbing because he does not fit the normal theology of "the
two ways." Bildad asks Job if he is willing to destroy traditional thinking.

Wisdom Literature states general principles (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: WISDOM LITERATURE) but Job's case is not covered. It is hard
for humans to recognize that they do not fully understand the mysteries
of fallen human existence. When we begin to think that our theology is
God's theology, all humility and teachability is gone, only arrogance
and dogmatism remain!

Job is living out his theology but they are simply mouthing theirs
(i.e., the unalterable nature of "the two ways").

18:5-21 This extended strophe
characterizes the plight of the godless, faithless person. Remember, Job
is not part of the covenant people, but the later sage who wrote these
dialogues assumed the covenant of Moses as the frame around the theology
of the Edomites.

I will list the consequences of wickedness (cf. Job 18:21; 8:11-19;
15:20-35) in outline forms, but remember this tends to remove the
powerful Semitic parallelism.

- their light goes out, Job 18:5 (cf. Job 21:17; Prov. 13:9; 20:20; 24:20)

- their understanding

- their life (b. is more probable)

- their tent is dark, Job 18:6 (possibly refers to descendants, cf. Job 18:16-17)

- their vigor is reduced, Job 18:7a

- their own schemes against others come back on them (i.e., OT reversals), Job 18:7b

- Job 18:8 repeats the thought of #4

- the imagery of Job 18:9 repeats that of #4

- the hunting imagery of Job 18:8-10 continues

- they are surrounded by fear and trembling, Job 18:11 (cf. Job 18:12b; 15:21,24)

- their strength is gone, Job 18:12a (cf. contrast in 17:9)

- they are diseased by "the King of Terrors" (a Ugaritic mythological
allusion to Mot, AB, p. 126), Job 18:13-14

- all their possessions are gone, Job 18:15

- they are described as a dead plant, Job 18:16 (cf. Job 15:30; Ezek. 17:9; Hos. 9:16)

- their memory perishes from the earth, Job. 18:17

- they are driven from the land of the living to the land of the dead, Job 18:18

- they have no posterity, Job 18:19 (same as #12)

- they become a proverb of horror for all peoples, Job 18:20

18:7

NASB, NRSV, JPSOA
"schemes"

"counsel"

The MT has "schemes" (BDB 420 I), but KB (KB 867) suggests
there is another root which means "disobedience" or "rebellion"
(NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 485).

18:12

NASB, NKJV
"at his side"

NRSV
"for their stumbling"

TEV
"at their side"

NJB

JPSOA

The MT has the MASCULINE SINGULAR NOUN (BDB 854).
This root has several meanings.

- rib, side

- limping, stumbling

Job is asserting that hunger and calamity are at his side. This has caused
his strength to fail.

18:13a This is an obvious
allusion to Job's condition. For the three friends, Job's disease and
disasters clearly reveal that he is a wicked person! These kinds of
things happen only to wicked people. God's word
has said! Prosperity is an evidence of obedience! But the "two ways" does
not cover every instance of evil and suffering in a fallen world.

18:13b "the firstborn of death"
This personification possibly refers to a demon.

SPECIAL
TOPIC: THE DEMONIC IN THE OLD TESTAMENT

18:14 "king of terrors"
Hebrew imagery has been affected by Ugaritic poetry (i.e., Ras Shamra
Texts). This does not assert the validity of this mythology, just its
powerful and well known imagery (cf. TEV). There are some hints of a
king of the underworld in Job 15:21; 20:21; Ps. 49:14 (shepherd as
royal imagery).

Death is often personified in the OT (cf. 2 Sam. 22:5,6; Ps. 7:13; 18:4;
116:3; Prov. 13:14; 14:27; Jer. 9:21; 18:21). This is imagery not
mythology. See G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, pp.201-271.

18:15a This line of poetry is
ambiguous. There are three options.

- It is imagery for the Mosaic curse that foreigners will occupy one's home and land.

- ANE imagery of wild animals living in human ruins (they often denoted the demonic,
cf. Isa. 13:21; 34:11-15).

- Similar wording from Ugaritic may make Job 18:15a parallel to 18:15b by translating it
as "fire resides in his tent" (UBS Handbook, p. 343, quoting Dahood's suggestion).

18:18 "into darkness" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEOL, I. B.

18:20 "in the west. . .in the east"
This imagery could refer to

- people who lived in different parts of the ANE (i.e., geography)

- people who lived before and those who came after (i.e., time, cf. JPSOA, Peshitta)

18:21 This is a summary verse.
Bildad means for it to apply to Job!

This general statement may explain the PLURAL of Job 18:2a. Job is seen
as part of a group (i.e., the wicked).

▣ "him who does not know God"
See
SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- To what saying of Job is Bildad reacting in Job 18:3?

- Explain Job 18:4 in your own words.

- Who is "the firstborn of death" in Job 18:13?

- Who is "the king of terrors" in Job 18:14?

- To whom is Job 18:20 referring?
